content: Excessive daytime sleepiness is a frequent symptom observed in individuals with myotonic dystrophy. Psychostimulant medications are increasingly being utilized as a treatment option for hypersomnia in these patients. The objective of this study was to systematically identify and synthesize evidence from randomized trials that assess the effects of psychostimulants in patients with myotonic dystrophy who experience hypersomnia. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Specialized Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies published up to October 2010. Additionally, the bibliographies of relevant papers were reviewed, and the authors of these studies were contacted for further information. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized or quasi-randomized trials that evaluated any type of psychostimulant, compared to either a placebo or no treatment, in children or adults with confirmed myotonic dystrophy and hypersomnia. Two authors independently reviewed potentially relevant studies, and a third author confirmed the selection of eligible trials. Data extraction was performed by one author and verified by another to ensure accuracy. The primary outcome assessed was the mean improvement in the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test (MWT). Data from two of the five identified trials, involving a total of 48 participants, were available for this outcome. The mean difference in MWT scores was +2.52 (95% confidence interval: -2.32 to +7.37), which was not statistically significant. Furthermore, there was considerable variability between the studies, as indicated by an I² value of 50%. Secondary outcomes included the mean improvement in the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), which was reported in four trials involving 101 participants. The mean difference in ESS scores was -2.26 (95% confidence interval: -3.78 to -0.73), favoring modafinil as a treatment. This result was statistically significant, but there was substantial heterogeneity across the studies, with an I² value of 84%. No evidence was found to suggest any treatment benefit on the Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) or on measures of quality of life. The authors concluded that there is low-quality evidence from two small trials indicating that psychostimulants do not significantly improve wakefulness as measured by the MWT in patients with myotonic dystrophy. However, there is low-quality evidence from four studies suggesting that modafinil significantly improves scores on the ESS. Further randomized trials are necessary to better evaluate the efficacy and safety of psychostimulants in this patient population.
